#9795. SealedBench: A Protocol for Freezing AI Benchmarks Before the Questions Are Known

A frozen model manifest, a generator sealed with drand, and an Arweave record anyone can use to rebuild the exam and check its scores.

On 2026-10-17, a bundle carrying my encrypted generator reached an Arweave block. The generator was sealed to a drand round that had not been published yet. I wrote that program, so I knew it would produce integer word problems, short Python programs, and shortest-path questions. I did not know which ones. The questions depended on a beacon the drand network would publish later, at round 33170212, on 2026-10-18T09:00:00Z.

When the round arrived, the same beacon value unlocked the program and seeded it. Four open-weight models answered 360 completions each: 240 on newly generated questions and 120 on a frozen set of public GSM8K items.

But the first two batches I ran should not be cited, and it is worth saying why, because the reason is the most useful thing in this article.

The first batch, b1, was valid under its own release record. Its manifest bound the ciphertext with a SHA-256 hash, but it never bound the ciphertext's transaction ID. Calling that check a pass would be a mistake, and it is WEAK. The v2 protocol exists partly to close that gap.

The second batch, b2, fixed the binding and then failed on the grader. The rule I sealed said an integer answer counts only when the last line is #### followed by nothing but the number. llama.cpp writes its end-of-text marker onto that same line, as #### 392 [end of text]. The registered grader threw the whole line away. Most of b2's arithmetic and GSM8K scores measure that rejection, not the rate at which models produced correct integers.

The ciphertext was already sealed by then, and the grader could not be changed in place. That constraint is the entire point of the protocol, and it applies to me too. So I made b3: a new commitment, sealed before its own round, with the normalization written into the scorer the manifest hashes.

So if you want a number from this project, take one from b3, and take the registered primary accuracy, which counts an answer as wrong when it cannot be parsed and wrong when the output was truncated. Its index transaction is vlVlUfyBn4IUmbXjkSX8079QuySP-Qqr8rN8TbivzTg. That index was published after the run. It is a convenient entry point, not evidence: the evidence that the generator existed before the round is the earlier ciphertext and manifest.

Public benchmarks leak. Once the questions are online, a high score may only mean the model has seen them.

A private test set looks like the fix, but it hands the same power to one person: whoever writes, stores, selects and reports the questions. That person includes the evaluator, which is me. If I can see the scores and then quietly change the seed, the prompt, the model file, or simply decide which batch to tell you about, I can aim the headline wherever I want.

SealedBench tries to pin all of that down in advance. The generator, the model hashes, the prompts, the runtime settings and the scoring code are bound to one future beacon round. Unless drand's operators reach a threshold and collude to compute that round early, I cannot read the beacon before it is published. If the network stops, the batch never opens; that is the other half of the bargain. After the round, anyone can rebuild the questions from the Arweave record and re-score the answers I published.

Here is every move I could make, and what I gave up in advance to make it visible.

Ciphertext and manifest on Arweave before the round

Check L1 block time, not the upload receipt

A hash cannot show which process wrote a file

Encryption cannot force me to publish answers

The manifest freezes the drand chain hash and public key, the release round, the seed rule, a SHA-256 for every GGUF, the llama.cpp commit and build flags, the prompts, the decoding settings, the grader and the reporting policy. Every batch uses quicknet chain 52db9ba70e0cc0f6eaf7803dd07447a1f5477735fd3f661792ba94600c84e971, genesis at unix 1692803367, period 3 seconds.

The generator is sealed to that round with drand time-lock encryption (tlock). The ciphertext and the manifest go up through the Turbo bundler. A receipt is not a commitment. The commitment is the L1 block.

Under the v2 rule a batch is valid only if the block holding its bundle is timestamped no later than unlock_unix − 600, the bundle ID appears in that block, and the data item's bytes hash to the committed SHA-256. Height, timestamp and block hash must agree on two independent gateways, and my own gateway ario.zigza.xyz does not count as either one. b1 used an earlier, simpler rule: manifest and ciphertext had to be in an L1 block before the release round, and a miss made the batch invalid, which I would still have had to report.

After the round, the beacon signature is checked against quicknet's fixed public key. The same beacon both decrypts the generator and enters the seed. One value doing two jobs is not two independent draws, and I do not claim otherwise.

b1's seed is a SHA-256 over a domain string, the chain hash, the round in decimal and the beacon randomness, with hex fields lowercased first. The exact sentence is in b1's manifest. v2 batches add a 32-byte secret stored inside the ciphertext, and hash length-prefixed fields: domain, chain hash, round, signature bytes and that secret. The JSON randomness field is not an input; it must still equal the SHA-256 of the signature. I chose the secret. It does not let me list the questions before the beacon exists. A successful tle -d only shows the ciphertext opens under the signature it was sealed to. The BLS check against the fixed public key is a separate step.

There is one specific gap in v1 worth naming. The November capsule cap and b1 share the same plaintext tarball, SHA-256 e054f1ab7824fde33e6ac399252098cf25c29815ff4ffacabbd311da05eac9c2. Once b1 opened, that program was public. Until 2026-11-15 the unknown is the beacon, not the program. v2 still hides its questions, because the secret sits inside the ciphertext.

Every family has a program for an oracle, so grading is code and not a judge model. arith_word produces two-to-five-step integer word problems; the oracle is a function of the sampling parameters, and the prompt contains no answer line. code_output produces short Python programs with no imports and no input, run in an interpreter with a step budget; the oracle is their stdout. graph_path asks for the weight of a shortest path on a random connected graph with edge weights from 1 to 9, always between nodes at least two edges apart; the oracle is Dijkstra.

The entropy check ran the generator over 1000 seeds and got 1000 distinct question sets, with 128,816 distinct prompts. That shows the seed changes the questions. It does not show the families are fair, or that they look unlike anything in training data. One caveat I want on the record: that check ran with a stand-in secret, not the sealed one, so it measures the generator's spread and not the exact bytes b2 and b3 committed.

All four models are official Q8_0 GGUFs, hashed locally against the published LFS object IDs before sealing:

Falcon3-1B is weak on purpose. It is a low anchor that makes a difficulty shift easier to see.

The runtime is llama.cpp v0.7.0, commit 620d2225cc436ab0b001e3200e590e3b286ef9ab, built CPU-only with AVX-512 on a Ryzen 7 7700 in a cgroup of about six CPUs and 18 GiB. Decoding is greedy: temperature 0, top-k 1, top-p 1, min-p 0, seed 42, -t 6 -b 2048 -ub 512.

Thread count and batch size are in the manifest because they change the output bytes. Repeated runs at -t 6 were byte-identical for all four models. Dropping to -t 4 changed 2 of 10 Qwen outputs. Changing to -b 512 -ub 128 changed Qwen, Gemma and Falcon. Ministral matched in all three comparisons. After release I replayed Qwen's first ten exam items: 10/10 byte-identical on b1, 10/10 on b2, 10/10 on b3. That is one model on one machine. Generating and grading are ordinary deterministic programs. I am not claiming your GPU would produce the same bytes.

120 arith, 60 code, 60 graph, plus GSM8K-test 0..119

80 arith, 30 code, 30 graph, plus GSM8K-test 0..79

80 arith, 30 code, 30 graph, plus GSM8K-test 0..79

Question-set SHA-256: b1 a91b6dab74eee35c8aaba81f8323610a5604fc7d73529bc7229aa3c6e1668193, b2 473acec24390a708a3323d51fe8a1cd2265591bcf8a4039f4564f49ab1833bdb, b3 549ba12a3062df5ce40393408d907544bbb9a2b75339b9ef6183015485fc9df3.

b1's release.json records batch_valid true. Its manifest 510sRNPxwIwK4D_xXkujpyih8M1pcww9DcZgOaLkkzU and ciphertext 57E6ydKUep6BKQ6L8wUSgrsDYkvq5r8pNmlUXzpxd7o entered block 2023266 at 2026-10-17T15:21:00Z, well before the unlock. Its index is AtNAZQtp_JqReahCoCpYcjP-b3P98jWtC_AJgVoBWdM. The v1 grader is not the v2 rule; it keeps a "take the last number" fallback. Arithmetic minus GSM8K, Wald 95%: Qwen 0.0083 [−0.0765, 0.0932], Gemma 0.1333 [0.0593, 0.2073], Ministral 0.1250 [0.0493, 0.2007], Falcon 0.4917 [0.3895, 0.5939]. Those two sets are not matched pairs.

b2's registered grader is sealedbench/v2/grade.py, SHA-256 98b796af643192968126a5895561ec1d4701c71ccf9af76ae874fe1f0b3b0648. The integer rule is ^####[ \t]+(-?\d[\d,]*)[ \t]*$. Code questions could still parse, because fenced-output extraction does not require the closing fence to own its line. On that registered endpoint Qwen scored 0/80 on arithmetic, with all 80 invalid, and 3/80 on GSM8K, with 76 invalid. Gemma and Ministral scored 0/80 on both integer families. Falcon scored 1/80 on arithmetic, 79 invalid. The raw files often already contained the right number; [end of text] was stuck to it.

The same scores.json carries a block called posthoc_sentinel_normalization, labelled POST-HOC with registered_primary false. It keeps the truncation rule on raw stdout and applies b3's normalization before the integer and code rules. There Qwen scores 73/80 on arithmetic and 77/80 on GSM8K. That is a reconstruction, not the score b2 promised to report.

b3 pins sealedbench/v2/grade.py and sealedbench/v2/grade_b3.py. The grader SHA-256 eab22119c837f790f900989ce7d3c8700635ad7881204ffc90079d800854b290 is a hash over both files sorted by path, not the hash of grade_b3.py alone. The registered normalization strips trailing ASCII whitespace, removes one trailing [end of text] if present, then strips again. Truncation is decided before that, on raw stdout. b3 has no post-hoc block. Its manifest is _aZZOYmKQr9awEhsmKew9J4sAHyDnfZoo1Pq1NYXOVk and its ciphertext MU3l3e_pbboAuVH8dtiLJP4XMGKGaFR530w-TauzteM.

v2 release files leave batch_valid unset. Their inclusion records put every sealed item's L1 time before that batch's own deadline. b2 and cap2 share bundle VWHJrEUcS-d9EXMzzJr9k6Qr2WKQLR9iwiMfm4nglgo, height 2023391, 2026-10-17T20:05:59Z. b3 and cap3 share J67Udct-eWBqCnNfoT9c_d0baY48io8tHlJ8uD_ZVys, height 2023739, 2026-10-18T08:11:02Z.

Primary accuracy, with invalid and truncated answers counted as wrong:

The Wilson 95% intervals behind the two columns in the figure, rounded to three decimals from the wilson95 arrays: Qwen arithmetic [0.800, 0.940] and GSM8K [0.895, 0.987]; Gemma [0.168, 0.355] and [0.232, 0.434]; Ministral [0.846, 0.965] and [0.713, 0.883]; Falcon [0.478, 0.689] and [0.179, 0.368].

Arithmetic minus GSM8K, Newcombe 95%: Qwen −0.075 [−0.166, 0.010], Gemma −0.075 [−0.211, 0.065], Ministral 0.1125 [0.007, 0.219], Falcon 0.325 [0.173, 0.457]. At n=80 near one half, a Wilson interval is roughly 11 points wide. A gap inside that width is the difference between two unmatched sets of questions. The fresh and public items differ in wording, length and format.

Calling that gap contamination would need a control this run does not have. One overlap should be stated plainly: Phase 1 had already run the models on GSM8K-test items 0..49, and b3's reference set covers 0..79, so the first 50 reference items were familiar ground before b3 was sealed. Nothing in this run separates that familiarity from the ordinary difficulty difference between two unmatched question sets.

Two cells deserve more than a headline. Qwen's graph score is 9/30, and 21 of those 30 outputs were truncated; across that family it produced 15 distinct answers, against a uniform-guess baseline of 0.067. Gemma's arithmetic is 20/80 with 60 invalid, and all 20 that parsed were correct; it produced 67 distinct answers, against a uniform-guess baseline of 0.015.

Figure 2 — b3 registered primary, fresh arith_word against GSM8K-test 0..79, with Wilson 95% intervals and n=80. article/fig/fig2_fresh_vs_public.png.

One complete example, taken from the first line of results/batches/b3/items.jsonl rather than picked for its score. Item arith_word-0000, template buy_give_price, oracle 392:

Gina buys 7 packs of balloons. Each pack has 9 balloons. Gina then gives 7 balloons to Kira. Each balloon is worth 7 dollars. How much are Gina's balloons worth in dollars?

Qwen's stdout is 294 bytes, 94 generated tokens, return code 0, not truncated, SHA-256 e2f21c8f5596848bc8b9e7c4991dcc72c7ccf79a3c77bc035538bb8dc1878b24. It ends with #### 392 [end of text]. b3 strips the marker and parses 392, detail match. The same bytes are invalid under b2's registered grader, detail no #### line. The file is results/batches/b3/runs/qwen3-4b-instruct-2507/arith_word-0000.txt.

I measured four Turbo bundles. The 20 probes from the first day are one bundle, not 20 latency samples. Latency here is the L1 block timestamp minus the earliest receipt time in that bundle.

ppP0MDrvyDX0uCeDTVww7FC4iGbkcbZiIazuQrcSIWE

pzzVUc5WUQHkZMWHu3D12AseYrj6ZSwH1nx9lKurvxk

VWHJrEUcS-d9EXMzzJr9k6Qr2WKQLR9iwiMfm4nglgo

J67Udct-eWBqCnNfoT9c_d0baY48io8tHlJ8uD_ZVys

Sorted: 193, 396, 518, 924. With linear interpolation at index (n-1)*p, p50 is 457 seconds and p95 is 863 seconds; the maximum is 924. Nothing in this sample was still pending. Later results and index uploads are not in it, and their block times were not recorded the same way.

The probes are 800 bytes each, sealed with tle v1.2.0 to rounds between 1176 and 1403 seconds after upload. Both the Go tool and tlock-js 0.9.0 refused to decrypt early, in 40 of 40 attempts. All 20 Turbo receipts verified. All 60 RFC 3161 timestamps from FreeTSA, DigiCert and Sectigo verified with openssl ts -verify. After the unlock, 20 of 20 probes decrypted in both tools and matched their plaintext hashes. FreeTSA's genTime landed a median 76.2 seconds after the Turbo receipt.

A GraphQL poller pointed at arweave.net ran for three hours and got HTTP 429 every time, observing nothing. Serving bytes, being in a block and being indexed are three different states. The commitment is the block. When arweave.net returns 404, the honest output is UNKNOWN.

Figure 3 — receipt-to-inclusion ECDF, one point per bundle, n=4. article/fig/fig3_inclusion_ecdf.png.

The repository is https://github.com/zigengZ/sealedbench, released as v1.0.0. You need Python 3.12 and Node.js 22. Leave SEALEDBENCH_ROOT unset.

Exit code 0 is PASS, 1 is a hard failure, and 2 is UNKNOWN, INVALID or WEAK. HTTP 404, 429 and timeouts all count as UNKNOWN. The command only reads gateways; it never uploads. It checks the published bytes, the inclusion deadline, the beacon signature and the grader hash, re-scores the published outputs, then decrypts the local ciphertext and rebuilds the question files. v2 requires https://ar-io.dev and https://turbo-gateway.com to agree. https://arweave.net takes no part in this check.

On 2026-10-24 a fresh clone of the release candidate printed RESULT PASS, exit code 0, in 26.15 seconds. The registered file results/batches/b3/verify_seal.txt still ends RESULT UNKNOWN, because ar-io.dev returned HTTP 404 for the manifest that day. The later file verify_recheck_20261024.txt ends PASS. An earlier attempt the same day was UNKNOWN. I did not overwrite the registered file with the later result.

b2's registered verify_seal.txt is UNKNOWN as well: the published scores and Ministral's completions returned 404. Its dated recheck is PASS. b1 was VALID in its 2026-10-18 release record, and the ciphertext-transaction-ID check is still WEAK. A b1 recheck on 2026-10-24 was never completed. From 2026-10-24T09:19:57Z every request this host made to arweave.net came back HTTP 429, including three attempts at b1's index. I stopped and did not restart it.

Replaying the model is the heavier second path. It needs the GGUF and the frozen llama-completion binary:

The registered replay directory is stamped 20261019T181448Z: 10 items compared, 10 byte-identical. The 2026-10-24 run compared 5 and matched 5, from arith_word-0000 to arith_word-0004. The weights were already on disk (qwen3-4b-instruct-2507-q8_0.gguf, 4,280,403,520 bytes). /usr/bin/time -v reported 1:05.87 wall clock, 337.29 seconds of user time, and a maximum resident set of 4,553,836 kB. During the process, the host's non-loopback interface counters rose by 185,159,022 bytes. That figure is for the whole host, not this command's downloads. SEALEDBENCH_ROOT was still pointing at another worktree, so the summary JSON was written there; the module that ran was the clone.

Byte-identical output means this recipe, on this machine, produces that stdout. It does not mean the original file was produced this way. A weight hash is not an execution attestation.

drand is an assumption. A threshold of operators could collude to compute a future round early. If the network stopped, the capsules would never open.

I know the question families. I know v2's secret. The entropy check shows new seeds give new questions. It cannot show the families are fair, or that the templates are absent from training data.

Decryption does not compel me to publish model answers. Declaring batches in advance makes a missing batch visible. It does not force me to release the answers.

The gap between fresh arithmetic and GSM8K is not a contamination measurement.

b2's registered integer scores are an artifact of the end-marker rule. The post-hoc block is labelled. b3 is the correction made after registration.

Closed models are outside this protocol. I cannot see their weights or their serving stack.

Once a round is published, anyone can copy its questions. The next batch needs a new round.

Very little of the machinery here is new on its own. Commitments, beacons, encrypted test sets and generated variants all exist. What I think is new is binding them into one scheduled future release and shipping the evidence.

A batch generated by a sealed generator at a scheduled future round

The generator is sealed to the same round that seeds it

Regularly refreshed questions with objective grading

Explicit pre-release commitments per batch

Decentralized AI Needs Decentralizable Trust (2026-06-29)

A small implementation with on-chain artifacts

Pre-release handling of questions, not decision receipts

Why AI Governance Needs a Decentralized Quality Assurance Layer (2026-09-01)

A smaller first version whose artifacts any reader can check

Someone else rebuilding a batch on another machine, without me. Larger batches declared in advance, with failures published beside successes. A fixed reference model to track difficulty across batches, without calling it formal equating. Several authors committing a larger pool before a later public draw. A threat model for vendors submitting their own answers, with timing evidence from independent witnesses. A batch registry on an AO process, but only if it adds a property this design lacks.

What remains is a checkable claim. For each published batch you can verify what was committed, when it was committed, which beacon released it, which questions it produced, and how the published answers score.

#9794. Validating 10,000-Row CSV Uploads in 20ms Before Touching Your Server (React + IndexedDB)

Watch someone import a 10,000-row billing CSV over spotty Wi-Fi on a standard web app. They pick the file, wait ten seconds for the progress bar to crawl to 100%, and get bounced back by a red toast: 400 Bad Request: Invalid amount on row 7,500. So they fix row 7,500, re-upload the entire file, and discover another typo on row 8,102.

If their connection drops while they are editing rows in your UI and they refresh the page, things usually get worse. A lot of apps try to stash draft uploads in localStorage, forget that browsers cap localStorage around 5 MB and block the main thread synchronously on writes, and end up throwing QuotaExceededError right when the user needs a backup most.

We can fix both problems on the frontend without pulling in a 200 KB validation library. In the companion repo (github.com/endlessfountain/react-offline-sheet-guard ), I wired up a small TypeScript preflight check that validates 10,000 CSV rows (40,000 cells) in 20.11 ms before a single byte hits the network, paired with a 45-line IndexedDB helper so multi-megabyte drafts survive offline refreshes.

Checking whether an email looks valid or whether seatCount is an integer is cheap. The line that quietly kills browser performance on 10,000-row sheets is duplicate ID detection.

When people write quick client-side validators, they often reach for Array.prototype.some() inside a row loop:

At 200 rows you won't notice. At 10,000 rows, scanning previousRows on every line turns into ~50 million comparisons and locks the tab for nearly a second on mid-range laptops. Swapping that array scan for a Set keeps duplicate detection O(1) per row (src/engine/sheetValidator.ts):

Notice that rowClean keeps checking all four columns on the same row instead of continue-ing after the first bad cell. If row 318 has both a broken email and "$1200" with a dollar sign, the user gets both errors at once rather than fixing the email, re-running, and getting yelled at a second time for the amount column.

Running npm test in the repo generates a 418.8 KB, 10,000-row CSV with four planted errors (duplicate ID at row 50, bad email at row 500, "$1200" at row 2,500, and 3.5 seats at row 7,500):

First, client preflight checks are purely a UX and bandwidth win, not a security boundary. Keep the exact same validation rules on your backend endpoint because anyone can send malformed payloads straight to your API with curl.

Second, line.split(",") only works when none of your columns legitimately contain commas inside quotes. As soon as you add a free-text companyName column containing values like "Acme, Inc.", switch the parser step to an RFC-4180 parser such as PapaParse so quoted commas don't shift your columns right by one index.

Finally, while 10,000 rows finishes in 20 ms on the main thread, 150,000 rows takes around 300 ms, which is long enough to make typing feel sluggish if you validate on every keystroke. Above 25,000 rows, either debounce validation by 250ms or move validateInvoiceSheet inside a Web Worker.

The column-shift case deserves more than a footnote, because it fails in the dangerous direction: "Acme, Inc." doesn't produce an error, it moves every later cell one column right, so an amount can pass validation as a seat count. Loud parse errors are annoying; silent realignment is a billing bug. The benchmark fixture plants four errors, all in flat unquoted cells, so both the 20ms and the 4/4 catch rate are proven against the case the parser already handles - plant one quoted-comma row and the suite starts guarding the switch to RFC-4180 instead of just recommending it. One more trap for that switch: rowNumber is currently a physical line index. Once quoted fields can contain newlines, logical records and physical lines diverge, and "fix row 7,500" starts pointing at the wrong row exactly when the file got harder.

#9793. New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

#9790. A Practitioner's Field Guide to Marketing Engineering

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

My name is Kristina Vislianska. I'm a growth marketer with 10+ years in B2B and B2C SaaS, AI, and Web3, and for the last couple of years, most of what I ship isn't campaigns. It's systems that run campaigns.

At some point, recruiters and founders started calling this "marketing engineering." I had to Google it. Turns out I'd been doing it for a while; I just called it "building stuff so I don't lose my mind doing the same thing every Monday."

This guide is for marketers who want to build, founders who want to hire someone who builds, and engineers who wonder what marketers are doing with their Claude or Codex Pro Max. Everything here comes from systems I built and ran, including the ones that broke.

Marketing engineering turns repeatable go-to-market work into software, combining marketing judgment with engineering skills. Its systems listen to the market, turn what they hear into content, distribute it, and learn from the results. A marketing engineer's output is not a campaign. It's the machine that produces campaigns.

The deliverable is a monitor, a pipeline, an agent or a feedback loop. Something that keeps working when you close your laptop.

And no, it's not "marketing that uses AI tools." Asking ChatGPT for ten hooks is using a tool. Marketing engineering starts when the work keeps running without you typing.

The title keeps changing. A few years ago it was "growth hacker," then "marketing technologist," now "GTM engineer" and "marketing engineer." Honestly, I don't think the title will survive. The skill will.

Marketing ops runs the machine. A GTM engineer builds the machine for sales. A marketing engineer builds the machine for attention. The three roles overlap, and the job titles are still a mess, so here's how I draw the lines.

Marketing ops keeps the existing stack working: clean CRM data, campaign setup, attribution reports. Success looks like data you can trust.

GTM engineers build the revenue engine for sales: enrichment, outbound sequences, lead routing. Success looks like meetings booked and pipeline.

Marketing engineers build the systems that create and distribute marketing: listening tools, content pipelines, community monitors, AI search presence, agents. Success looks like reach, citations in AI answers, and how much one person can run.

Think of a restaurant. Marketing ops keeps the kitchen clean and the orders flowing. The GTM engineer builds the delivery system that gets food to customers who already ordered. The marketing engineer builds the thing that makes people walk past and want to come in. Usually a marketing engineer combines the roles of a whole team of specialists. I like to call them the king of agents and systems.

Everything I've built fits into one of five layers: Listen, Understand, Make, Ship and Learn. I call it the marketing engineering loop, because what you learn at the end changes what you listen for at the start.

Here's the thing most teams get wrong. They start with Make, because "AI writes posts" is the obvious use case. But content volume was never the bottleneck. In my experience the biggest gains sit in Listen and Learn. Listening finds the moments worth acting on. Learning tells you which of your actions actually mattered.

Automate tasks that repeat often and are safe to get wrong. For tasks that repeat often but happen in public, let the machine draft and keep a human on the send button. I call this the frequency × risk matrix.

The most common mistake I see is automating whatever is easiest to automate. That's how you end up with a bot that confidently replies to a grieving customer with a discount code. Two questions work much better: how often does this task repeat, and how bad is it if the machine gets it wrong in front of people? The answer is a split: the machine finds and drafts, a person approves and sends.

Theory is nice, but you came here for the real stuff. Here's one system for each layer of the loop, with what it taught me.

Situation. I wanted to find advisory clients without cold pitching. I hate cold pitching, and so does everyone receiving it. The best moment to talk to a founder is when they post "we just raised" or complain that growth has stalled. Those posts disappear from the feed in hours.

What I built. A radar that searches Threads for pain-point phrases in English and trigger phrases in Ukrainian, like "we raised" or "we got our first revenue." For every match it drafts a reply and pings me in Telegram or email. I read it, rewrite it if needed, and post it myself. The system never posts on its own, and nobody gets a pitch in the first message.

What it taught me. Listening is the cheapest layer to automate and the most valuable. Timing beats copy.

Situation. At an AI workflow automation platform, we were selling agents to small service businesses in seven verticals. To sell to them, we needed to know which tools they already use and what actually makes them swear at their phones.

What I built. A research system that produces three things per vertical: an integration map of the software they already use, a pain-point file built from scraped Reddit threads and classified by an LLM, and ready-made agent templates that solve the top pain with the tools they already have. The research didn't just shape the message. It turned into the product itself: the templates.

What changed. Cost per lead dropped by 80%. Instead of guessing, we shipped 7 agent templates, one per vertical, each built around a pain owners described in their own words. Our one-size-fits-all pitch was gone.

What it taught me. Research is the cheapest way to lower acquisition cost. Before you spend another dollar on ads, find out how your buyers describe their pain. And the same research that shapes your message tells the product team what to build next.

Situation. We needed explainer videos for all seven verticals. We had no video team and no budget to hire one.

What I built. A pipeline where a script goes in and a finished video comes out. The script is split into lines. A voice API generates the voiceover for each line as a separate audio file. Remotion, a React framework for video, renders each scene, and the length of each audio file sets the length of its scene. The on-screen graphics come from a custom skill that holds our whole design system, so every frame follows our brand style guide.

What changed. Seven verticals covered without hiring a single editor. One agent turns a script into a finished, on-brand video in 15 minutes. The pipeline produced 5 videos a day at under $1 each, a fraction of what an agency charges.

What it taught me. When a video costs less than a dollar and 15 minutes, it stops being a project and becomes an experiment. You can test messages in video the way you test headlines. The bottleneck moves from production to knowing what to say, which is exactly why the Listen and Understand layers come first.

Situation. Outreach on X works best when you show up in the right conversation at the right moment. Doing that by hand means scrolling for hours, hoping to catch the one post where someone describes exactly the problem you solve. And by the time you've written a good reply, the moment is gone.

What I built. A browser extension for X that finds outreach opportunities by keywords and trigger phrases, like someone announcing a launch, asking for a tool recommendation or complaining about a problem. When it finds a match, a ready-made prompt system drafts the reply for me in my voice. I read it, tweak it if needed, and send it myself. Every reply gets logged, so the system learns which triggers and formats actually start conversations.

What changed. 20 targeted replies a day, without losing my whole morning. Instead of scrolling for an hour to find two good posts, I review a list of drafts, each tied to a real trigger, and spend my time only on the human part. The logs show which triggers start conversations and which just collect polite likes, so the keyword list gets sharper every week.

What it taught me. Automating Learn isn't about saving time. It's about running enough experiments to see what a platform rewards and punishes. A handful of manual replies will never show you that.

Tools change every few months. These six principles haven't changed across anything I've built, and most of them I learned by breaking something.

You don't need a computer science degree. You climb four rungs: Operator, Assembler, Builder and Architect. Each one needs a different skill, and most marketers get stuck between the second and the third.

Full honesty: I don't write Python from memory. I build with Claude Code and Cursor. What I can do is read the code, understand why it broke, and explain to the AI what to fix. That's the real skill.

The jump from Assembler to Builder isn't about learning to write code. It's about learning to read it well enough to tell why it stopped working at 3 a.m.

Your best first project? Your most boring weekly task. Build the system, put yourself on the send button, and measure what you learn, not the time you save. That's the whole discipline in miniature.

Is marketing engineering the same as growth hacking? No. Growth hacking was about finding clever tactics. Marketing engineering is about building durable systems that run those tactics repeatedly and learn from the results.

Do marketing engineers need to know how to code? They need to read code, not necessarily write it from scratch. With AI coding tools like Claude Code or Cursor, the bottleneck is understanding what broke and why.

What tools do marketing engineers use? Usually LLM APIs, Python or JavaScript, scrapers, no-code automation tools, voice and video AI, etc. The specific tools matter less than the loop they form.

What is the difference between a marketing engineer and a GTM engineer? A GTM engineer builds systems that turn buying signals into sales pipeline. A marketing engineer builds systems that turn market signals into reach, content and visibility.

What should a company automate first in marketing? Tasks that repeat weekly and are safe to get wrong, like monitoring, research and reporting. Public-facing tagive me sks like replies and outreach should be drafted by machines and sent by humans.

Will AI replace marketers? AI replaces repetitive marketing tasks, not marketing judgment. Deciding what to automate, what to say and when a process is broken is still a human job.

Marketing engineering is not about making more content faster. AI already solved that, and honestly, the internet didn't need more of it. It's about building systems that know where to listen, what to say, where to ship it and what to learn from it, while you keep the judgment.

The tools will keep changing. The judgment about what's worth automating is the part that stays yours.

Which layer of the loop have you automated already, and which one do you think is overrated? Tell me in the comments. I read all of them, without a bot.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

#9787. Payment-native from day one — building with QRIS in Indonesia

Posted on Nov 8 • Originally published at ksatriabintangsamudra.com

Most payment tutorials assume a credit card and a Western checkout. In Indonesia that assumption quietly blocks a huge share of your users. The default here is QRIS — one QR standard that every bank and e-wallet accepts. If your product can't take a QRIS payment, for many people it simply can't take their money.

The single most important thing about payments is also the easiest to get wrong: the client is not allowed to decide that a payment succeeded. A "payment complete" message in the app is a UI state, not a fact. The fact lives on the server, confirmed against the payment provider.

If the app crashes, if the webhook is spoofed, if the user closes the tab — the truth is still correct, because it was never the client's to decide.

Two things bite everyone building payments:

Building payment-native isn't just a technical nicety here — it's the difference between a product Indonesians can actually use and one they can't. QRIS removes the card requirement, the foreign-currency friction, and the sign-up-for-a-processor barrier. The engineering discipline — server-side truth, idempotency, transactional settlement — is what keeps it trustworthy once real money is moving.

Money is the one place where "it works on my machine" is never good enough. Verify on the server, make it idempotent, settle it in the database.

#9786. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9785. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.
